account: Malawi's June 2017 measles vaccination campaign (Measles & Rubella Initiative) targeted more than 7.5 million children. The American Red Cross's Missing Maps team needed base maps for campaign monitoring. Facebook's population maps come from a machine-learning computer-vision method that detects buildings in satellite imagery. The team used them to identify where people lived and which areas were already mapped in OpenStreetMap. Concentrating volunteers on settlements filtered out 97.1% of the land area, reducing the area to map from 94,080 km² to 2,745 km². Volunteers completed the base map in a fraction of the normal time. The Red Cross article of 7 June 2017 predates the campaign and says that the base map was to feed a dashboard for government and Red Cross monitors. On 10 August 2017 the Missing Maps blog reported that the traced base map underpinned a real-time monitoring dashboard covering 13,743 children. The blog says that 3,000 local Malawi Red Cross volunteers made house-to-house visits in five districts, and it credits the Facebook data with faster remote tracing. No source reports an effect of the maps on vaccination coverage. In their own validation, the authors from Facebook and the Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) report a recall of 0.84 for the layer in a rural test area near Blantyre that Missing Maps volunteers had mapped by hand. In April 2019 Facebook restated the case and credited its maps with letting the Red Cross deploy 3,000 volunteers to specific areas.

ai_role.statement: The Facebook settlement data determined where volunteer mapping effort went and which areas were skipped. The campaign itself was a Measles & Rubella Initiative effort supported by the American Red Cross and other partners, with monitors from the national government. The Red Cross attributes efficiency, not coverage, to the maps. The Red Cross account is the implementing organization's and names only “Facebook's population datasets”, without mentioning machine learning. The identification with the High Resolution Settlement Layer and the machine-learning description are taken from the vendor-authored Tiecke et al. preprint. It does not mention the Malawi campaign.

comparator.against: mapping the whole national land area without the settlement maps (the normal Missing Maps approach)
comparator.quote: Much of Malawi is rural, so concentrating on population settlements allowed us to filter out 97.1% of the total land area that we sought to map. This technique reduced our mapping area from 94,080km2 to 2,745 km2. Volunteers could then spend their time mapping communities instead of searching through acres of uninhabited areas; they were able to complete the mapping in a fraction of the normal time.

fields.account: Malawi's June 2017 measles vaccination campaign (Measles & Rubella Initiative) targeted more than 7.5 million children. The American Red Cross's Missing Maps team needed base maps for campaign monitoring. Facebook's population maps come from a machine-learning computer-vision method that detects buildings in satellite imagery. The team used them to identify where people lived and which areas were already mapped in OpenStreetMap. Concentrating volunteers on settlements filtered out 97.1% of the land area, reducing the area to map from 94,080 km² to 2,745 km². Volunteers completed the base map in a fraction of the normal time. The Red Cross article of 7 June 2017 predates the campaign and says that the base map was to feed a dashboard for government and Red Cross monitors. On 10 August 2017 the Missing Maps blog reported that the traced base map underpinned a real-time monitoring dashboard covering 13,743 children. The blog says that 3,000 local Malawi Red Cross volunteers made house-to-house visits in five districts, and it credits the Facebook data with faster remote tracing. No source reports an effect of the maps on vaccination coverage. In their own validation, the authors from Facebook and the Center for International Earth Science Information Network (CIESIN) report a recall of 0.84 for the layer in a rural test area near Blantyre that Missing Maps volunteers had mapped by hand. In April 2019 Facebook restated the case and credited its maps with letting the Red Cross deploy 3,000 volunteers to specific areas.
